10044018:
Anne M. Gallaudet Scarborough, Maine
April 17, 2025
Re: LD 376, An Act to Improve Maternal and Infant Health Outcomes through Doula Care
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and Honorable Members of the Joint Health and Human Services Committee
I appreciate this opportunity to address you on this important matter. My name is Anne Gallaudet. I am a resident of Scarborough, Maine. I am writing in support of LD 376.
I support this bill because Maine hospitals are experiencing extensive financial strain. Some hospitals have closed entirely; others, although still operating, have closed their birthing units. The loss of birthing units has occurred disproportionally in rural areas. As a result, already underserved pregnant people find they must drive up to three hours to receive prenatal or postpartum care or birth their baby. Allowing reimbursement for doulas under MaineCare is an important tool to help address this crisis in maternity care that Maine is experiencing.
Access to care by doulas through MaineCare will undoubtedly have a positive impact on improving prenatal and postpartum mental and physical health and birth outcomes, reduce infant mortality rates and do so particularly for traditionally underserved people.
By the end of 2024, 18 states along with Washington, DC have implemented Medicaid coverage for doula care. Nine more states are in the process of implementing Medicaid coverage for doula care. These states are a collection of red, purple and blue states. https://www.badoulatrainings.org/blog/state-of-the-states-efforts-to-expand-access-to-doulacare-in-medicaid-and-private-insurance This is an area ripe for bipartisan support. Access to health care by providing doula services contributes to a positive prenatal, birthing and postpartum experience for pregnant people, and increases the chances a healthy baby is born.
My older daughter used a doula, along with her obstetrician, for both her pregnancies for perinatal care and raved about her experience. Indeed, with respect to her second child, she had the baby at home in 2016 with the help of only the doula and her husband. She felt the doula provided excellent emotional and educational support during the whole perinatal period, had supportive ideas for resolving physical issues that came up while pregnant, and aptly handled the birthing experience.
I urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 376.
Anne Gallaudet, Scarborough, ME

Senator lngwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and Human Services Committee, I am Senator Denise Tepler, representing Senate District #24, all of Sagadahoc County and the Town of
Dresden in Lincoln County. I am here today to present LD 376, "An Act to Improve Maternal and Infant
Health Outcomes Through Doula Care."
In 2022, my last session as the termed-out Representative from the Town of Topsham, I was fortunate to
be named National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) Maternal and Child Health Fellow. This meant a series of multi-day meetings both online and in person on topics in this area of health care. Of the series of actions that states were advised to take in order to improve equity and access to maternal and
infant health, increasing access to Doula care was the one policy Maine had not yet enacted. Many
disturbing statistics were shared at the meeting, illustrating that our wealthy and advanced nation is not taking goodcare of our mothers and babies. In fact, maternal and infant death rates in the U.S. are concerningly high compared to most other developed nations. I came away from that fellowship determined to try to expand access to Doulas in our state through MaineCare.
In 2023, I asked Representative Kristi Mathieson to sponsor a bill to this effect. She did so, but it would have taken more preparation and heart than could be spared for someone else's idea, so she withdrew the
bill over objections from the Doula associations. Now I am back, and I still feel strongly that Maine needs
to take this action. I understand that hearts and minds have changed in the Department, and there is grant
funding for this effort. I also understand that the loss of maternity care centers in many parts of rural Maine has deepened the need for Doula care. I further understand that the Maine Doula Association now supports this effort with several caveats I will discuss before the end of this testimony. And now, you
have 2 bills, this one and LD 1523, to choose from in moving this policy forward.
My bill was based on the New York State model -- the most recently passed state Doula care bill. I was
given to understand that Representative Dhalac's bill is based on the Massachusetts model. They are veiy
similar but differ slightly in the inclusion in that LD 1523 includes an advisory group, which I support.
These are both important bills, and I leave it to the committee and the Department to choose which model you prefer. Either will improve equity and access to maternal and infant health care.
There are three additional policies that need to be either made part of one of these bills or adopted in Depaitmental rule-making. These represent policies that the Maine Doula Association has studied and recommended,
1. Reimbursement for Doula Services must create a living wage. No Doulas will want to serve
the Mainecare population if this is not done.

10044295:
Testimony in Support of LD 1523: An Act to Provide MaineCare Coverage for Doula Services
Gina Caruso-Rissing Southwest Harbor, ME 04679 April 15, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and Honorable Members of the Health and Human Services Committee:
Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. My name is Gina Caruso-Rissing; I'm a resident of Southwest Harbor, ME and mother of two little girls, ages 2 years and 3 weeks. I am writing today in strong support of LD 1523.
This bill is an important step toward improving maternal and infant health outcomes across our state. Doula care has been consistently shown to reduce rates of cesarean birth, shorten labor, increase breastfeeding success, and improve the overall birth experience for families. Doulas offer nonclinical, culturally appropriate, and continuous physical, emotional, and informational support throughout pregnancy, birth, and the postpartum period.
I was fortunate enough to be able to pay out of pocket for doula support during my pregnancies, which ended up being high-risk due to preeclampsia. The care I received from my doulas was invaluable. They offered steady emotional grounding during uncertain moments and helped me navigate complex decisions. Their presence made an enormous difference--not only during labor but throughout the postpartum period, when support is often scarce and deeply needed.
I can say from personal experience that doula care improves outcomes in both quantifiable ways and in ways that are difficult to quantify but deeply felt. And yet, this kind of support is currently only accessible to those who can afford to pay privately. LD 1523 would help correct this inequity by requiring MaineCare to reimburse for doula services, expanding access to this vital support for families who need it most. Given the disparities in birth outcomes that persist across racial, geographic, and economic lines, expanding access to doulas is not just a healthcare issue--it's a matter of justice.
Investing in doulas is a cost-effective, evidence-based way to improve outcomes for parents and babies alike. I urge the committee to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 1523 and help make Maine a state where all families--regardless of income--can access the support they deserve during one of life's most vulnerable and transformative times.
Thank you for your time and for your consideration of this critical bill.
Sincerely, Gina Caruso-Rissing

Testimony ofRepresentative Holly Eaton in support of
LD 376, An Act to Improve Maternal and Infant Health Outcomes Through Doula Care
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and Human Services Committee, my
name is Representative Holly Eaton, and I represent House District 15, which includes a number of coastal, rural and island communities across Hancock County. I'm also a Certified Doula and a Licensed Massage
Therapist, and I'm here today in strong support of LD 376, An Act to Improve Maternal and Infant Health
Outcomes Through Doula Care, sponsored by Senator Tepler.
As a doula, I can speak to the unique role we play in supporting families through pregnancy, labor and the
postpartum period. Doulas are nonclinical professionals trained to provide continuous emotional, physical and
informational support. We do not replace nurses or rnidwives----we work alongside medical professionals to help the birthing person feel more confident, more informed and more at ease. We offer comfort measures like
breathing techniques or positioning during labor, help families understand what to expect and provide
consistent, compassionate presence throughout the birthing experience. We also support the transition to
parenthood in the weeks following birth.
In a system where birthing people may not have the same provider at every appointment or delivery, the ability to have a doula they trust and know can make a powerful difference. It creates a sense of continuity, security
and reassurance. LD 376 acknowledges this by ensuring reimbursement under MaineCare for up to four
prenatal visits, attendance at the birth and four postpartum visits with a doula. This kind of access is not just a
nicety--it's essential care.
We know that doula support improves health outcomes, lowers rates of complications and enhances the
emotional well--being of parents. This bill ensures more Mainers have the opportunity to receive that care-- especially those in rural, underserved and lower-income communities.
I am grateful to Senator Tepler for bringing this bill forward and to the cosponsors for recognizing how meaningful doula care can be. I urge you to support LD 376 and make this kind of support available to all Maine families who need it.

10044939:
Kathryn Norgang Portland LD 376
Good afternoon, My name is Kate Norgang, MSN-Ed., RN. I am a nurse working for Maine's health care system, an educator, and a maternal and public health worker with 23 years of experience caring for women and children. I also became a mother myself within the past year, and through this experience I learned first-hand how vulnerable families are during pregnancy, delivery, and aftercare.
I was fortunate to well cared for by an interprofessional team; some of this was available through Maine's healthcare system. Some I had to seek out and pay for, and I am privileged to do this. It truly made a difference when I experienced a sudden medical emergency, and the aftermath of acclimating to life as a new mom while recovering.
We are now thriving, only because we were able to draw upon a variety of support needed. Doula care, in addition to midwifery care, truly made the difference in keeping my family whole and healthy.
Doulas are a unique cadre of care professionals who work within the healthcare team to promote comfort, empowerment, and resilience among birthing people and their families. They are skilled, insightful, collaborative, and can act as a safety net-something that is essential in a time when our health care system is overstretched.
Every birthing person and family deserves access to the care doulas provide during pregnancy, delivery, and postpartum. MaineCare reimbursement for these services would allow more equitable access, and also the network of doula care to become more stable, which is key to ensuring these services will continue to exist.
In my current role working with underserved populations in Maine (rural, New Mainer migrant, refugee and asylum-seeking families, pregnant people in recovery, and those experiencing unstable housing), I have seen first-hand the impact that doula care can provide. We would love to connect every person birthing alone in Maine, every person struggling to make their healthcare appointments, every person who living in isolation, fear and overwhelm, with a doula. However, to do this there must be a pathway for service reimbursement.
I urge you to pass this essential bill, LD 376 - An Act to Improve Maternal and Infant Health Outcomes Through Doula Care, immediately. Let's give all people and families in Maine the evidenced based, crucial support needed for a healthy start with their new baby.

Re: LD 376 - An Act to Improve Maternal and Infant Health Outcomes Through Doula Care
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, thank you for the opportunity to provide information in opposition of LD 376, An Act to Improve Maternal and Infant Health Outcomes Through Doula Care.
This bill requires reimbursement under the MaineCare program for doula services by January 1, 2026. The Department agrees that doula services would provide additional prenatal, labor, and postnatal support to MaineCare members, and is already undertaking this work under a recent federal award to the Office of MaineCare Services, called "Transforming Maternal Health" (TMaH), described in more detail below. In addition, this bill, provides insufficient time to design and implement doula services and does not align with the timing or expectations of related work under TMaH. The TMaH workplan, partner engagement activities, and financial resources are necessary for the successful implementation of MaineCare coverage of doulas.
In January 2025, the Office of MaineCare Services was awarded participation in the TMaH model with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. All state Medicaid agencies participating in the TMaH Model are required to cover or have a concrete plan to cover doula services by the end of 2027. To get to the point of doula coverage, the Office of MaineCare Services will follow a defined workplan, beginning with the establishment of a Statewide Doula Council in mid-2025. This multidisciplinary, multisector Statewide Doula Council will be responsible for the identification of training and/or certification provider requirements and doula service delivery/coordination requirements. Broader work will be funded by the federal award to design outreach and education to the community at large about doula coverage through MaineCare.
Over the next number of years, in addition to this outreach and education, the Department will conduct a rate determination, request the appropriate federal approval, and conduct state rulemaking to implement doula coverage. The Department will also determine the need for state appropriation to align with more concrete implementation dates and reimbursement amounts.
The Department encourages the committee to support the Department's rollout of doula services as a component of the TMaH Model in alignment with approved federal cooperative agreement

timeline and with adequate appropriation. Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.
Sincerely,
Michelle Probert Director Office of MaineCare Services Maine Department of Health and Human Services
